hanks to Niva for getting us ‘rattled’ last month. It is quite the process she has designed and
I am looking forward to trying it for one of my family’s newborns. This was Niva’s first demo
and it shows that not just the ‘experts’ are capable of demonstrating. Maybe there is a topic
you would like to see demonstrated. Well do some research and then see Larry so he can get you on
the list for next year. I have.
We have a few committed volunteers who do not have people who can back them up if they miss a
meeting. If anyone is interested in helping out with the photography or the audio/visual, please let
me know. Both these positions contribute so much to the guild that it is imperative we have a few
people who know how things work.
With summer well on its way, this will be our last meeting until September. I hope everyone gets a
chance to do some turning. Maybe try something new. I have a project for you to work on. September’s President’s Challenge will be a cup and saucer. I know I can count on some of you to do something unusual, but the rest of us can practice our hollowing and gluing skills.
Have a great summer and Happy Turning!
Bill

Editor's Notes
This is the third edition from your new newsletter team. Robert and I continue to work through details and are discovering little things that will, hopefully, make the newsletter better. As before, any
suggestions you have are welcome.
I want to give a big thank you to Dennis and Kerry who do so much to photograph all the pieces
each month. And it is not just taking the pictures. There is lots of post processing work that Dennis
does to ensure we have excellent images to spruce up the newsletter. The original images are very
high quality so if you need one or more of them for your own promotions please let Dennis know.
In the past, the newsletter has been dormant through the summer break but I would like to try to
produce at least one issue over the break. If you have any events happening this summer that would
make good copy then please let me know. We can work together to get them in the summer issue.

Dave started us off this month with a report on
several pens that he turned and got laser engraved
by Steve Fairbairn. Other than the excellent job on
the pens and engraving Dave also mentioned that
one was a left-handed pen and the other was a
right-handed one. He explained that the engraving
on one was on the left side of the clip when looking
down the pen so a right-handed writer could read
it. For the leftie the engraving is on the right side
of the clip; a clever detail that I had not considered.
We grilled Steve a little about his laser engraver
where we learned that there are limitations to engraving on round things but with planning and
some ingenuity they can be overcome. This is especially true when your laser engraver is also a
Guild member. Email Steve at steve@stevemopolis.com if you have questions about
laser engraving your work.
Tom asked if the large “Coles” jaws from
Easywood.com would fit into Oneway chucks.
While none of us had a definitive answer it lead to
a discussion about making ones own jaws. Dennis
reminded us that Merv wrote an interesting article
in our May 2007 newsletter about doing just that.
I added that production bowl turner Dale Larson
had made a set of stepped jaws from wood. Visit
http://www.turnedwoodenbowls.com for an interesting article on making them. (Fig 4.1)
(Fig 4.1)
I also read a number of articles this month on making a Longworth Chuck. There is a nicely written
article at http://
www.woodworkersguide.com/2010/10/17/how-tomake-a-longworth-chuck/ that guides you through
the process. For those who enjoy making tools and
who plan to turn lots of bowls this is another possibility. (Fig 4.2)
(Fig 4.2)
We then talked about using a vacuum chucking
system instead of Coles jaws. For me, vacuum systems are as much an addition to woodturning as
was the scroll chuck. They offer quick reversing of
bowls including natural edge ones and expand your
ability to hold difficult pieces. We talked about using an oil-less vane pump to reduce contamination
in the air and for having a good filter system in the
line between your chuck and the pump. Wood is
relatively porous and the sanding dust is often
sucked right through the wood and into the vacuum line.
And it seems whenever we talk about vacuum
(Continued on page 5)
Bruce Campbell
Tech Talk

Page 5
GVWG
pumps we also talk about venturi pumps. Instead
of drawing air out of a closed space a venturi system blasts high pressure air through a narrow nozzle. A hose connected to the exit side of the nozzle
just after the narrowest part will draw a vacuum
(see fig 4.3). As many of us have compressors and
venturi nozzles are relatively inexpensive, this
might be an attractive alternative. The main concern is that these systems require a pretty significant air flow to keep them going. But, if that is
what you have then a venturi system might work
for you.
(Fig 4.3)
I recently had to hand sand several bowls that were
turned wet and were too warped to sand on the
lathe. I discovered that putting my 3” sanding pad
in my drill press make it a lot easier. The ability to
hold the bowl up to the moving sanding pad gave
me lots of control and it was easier on my back.
Steve commented that he does that too but puts
the sanding pad in a chuck with spigot jaws on his
lathe. He also cautioned that the Jacobs chuck in a
drill press often has a Morse taper that is not really
designed to withstand side pressure. Side pressure
can cause the MT to release from its socket. A reasonable solution to this it to have a draw bar securing for Jacobs chuck but not all drill presses allow
for that. I know mine does not.
Dan took us off in another direction by asking how
to colour epoxy. David suggested powdered pigments that he buys at Michaels’; Robert uses universal filler from Fiber Tech; and several recalled
that Marilyn Campbell used micro-filler and inexpensive oil-based paints. I recommend some testing before applying to your work as some interactions can slow down or even prevent certain epoxies from setting.
Finally, while not actually talked about in our session, Neva mentioned in her main presentation
that she uses large stainless steel turkey basters for
managing finishes. She replaced the rubber “O”
ring in the plunger with a neoprene one and draws
in a large quantity of finish. Then she is able to
dispense only what she needs and the remainder
stays in an air-tight environment which prevents it
going off. What a clever idea.
I hope you found something useful this time and
hope to see you at the next Tech Talk.
Free Harwood Off-cuts
A furniture maker in East Vancouver is interested
in finding a good home for some of his small offcuts. These are too small for his use but still quite
usable for smaller turnings. He has Maple, Cherry
and Walnut and occasionally some exotic hardwoods and is offering them for free. In you are interested please contact:
Jay Miron at jay@jaymiron.com

Looking over the
Instant Gallery table at the May
meeting Phil Vetra’s
“Tribute to Binh
Pho” really did
stand out. That was
partly because of
the elegant way it
was displayed on a
mirrored stand but
also because of its
vibrant colours and simple yet subtle shape. Before I even knew the title, the piece screamed “Binh
Pho”, the Chicago-based wood turner who, along
with the late Frank Sudol of Saskatchewan, literally
defined a new woodturning genre of thin-walled,
pierced and air brushed vessels. Sudol often used
scenes of nature on his work while Pho developed a
unique set of imagery to tell stories of his remarkable life.
The challenge with working in an area that is so
clearly defined by one artist is trying to separate
your work from that artist. Many people feel that
just making a piece in a defined style somehow violates an implied “copyright”. Personally, I think
there is great value in copying artists you admire.
Copying great works of art is a long-standing method of learning and after sufficient study the diligent
student can take the lessons learned and extend
them into ways that are uniquely their own. The
only caveat is to not complete with the original artist by selling knock-offs of their work.
I applaud Phil for his piece and his clear declaration of its motivation. So let’s take a closer look…..
Phil has worked with wood all his life starting in
high school in Surrey. He built his own lathe in
1972 with pillow blocks and a simple spindle that
accepted faceplates. As some point he bought a
three-jawed machinist chuck to try to make things
easier but, in time he outgrew that lathe and purchased a General mini-lathe. Like a number of us,
he quickly outgrew that lathe too and finally
stepped up to a large Vicmarc in 2008 which he
turns on now.
Phil retired in 2005 and while looking for something to do found both the Fraser Valley and our
Guild and has been a member for several years.
When Fraser Valley brought in Binh Pho to
demonstrate, Phil planned to attend and take his
class. He even turned several small vessels in
preparation. But his part-time work schedule prevented him from taking the class. Instead, he had
(Continued on page 7)
Bruce Campbell
A Closer Look at
Phil Vetra’s “A Tribute to Binh Pho”

Page 7
GVWG
to settle on looking over peoples shoulders as best
he could (the class was at his part-time job site).
Afterwards, he went into his shop and applied what
he could remember to his piece. He told me that
the patterns are partly Binh’s but the layout is
Phil’s
Phil says that the project was very challenging with
lots of things to learn. The colours were applied
with an air brush and the piercing was done with
an NSK Presto hand piece. The unique stepped lip
is a strong Pho-ian element but Phil says the design on the three panels is his own salute to Pho,
his work, and his remarkable life of struggle, endurance, and success.
I hope we get to see more of this type of work from
Phil as he looks for ways to “make it his own”.
(Continued from page 6)

My interest in turning a baby rattle was triggered
by the birth of my nephew’s first child. I wanted to
buy something special to commemorate the birth
so I went to Birk’s and saw their sterling silver
dumbbell baby rattle. The more I thought about
this rattle the more I thought that I should be able
to turn it so over time I developed the following
steps. I know there are many different styles of
rattles and different ways to turn them but as a
novice turner I was not familiar with many of them
and so I came up with my own method. For variations on this method I refer you to the internet
where there is a lot of information and especially to
the AAW article in the February 2011 issue.
I discovered that there are Canadian and International guidelines for baby rattles. They require that
the rattle be constructed such that no part of it can
fit all the way through the opening of the rattle impaction test gauge. This requirement helps protect
an infant from taking part of a rattle into their
mouth and having it lodge in the back of their
throat obstructing breathing. The RATTLE IMPACTION TEST GAUGE which they refer to requires a dimension of no less than 1.68 inches
(42.7 mm) and requires that any removable part
withstand a force of 50 newtons (11.2 pound force)
or a torque of less than 1 newton metre (8.85 inch
pounds).
METHOD

Start with a blank measuring 8.5 inches (21.6
cm) long x 2.5 inches (6.35 cm) wide.

Place blank between centers and using a roughing gouge, round to about 1⅞ inches to 2 inches.

Make a tenon on both ends to fit chuck.

Use story board to mark dimensions.

Using a cut-off tool, cut down the markings for
the dumbells.

Rough out the middle portion which will be the
handle, being sure to leave enough bulk to keep
the block stable.

remove from between centers and place in
chuck and bring up the tailstock.

Using a spindle gouge rough out the shape of
the dumbells.

Using a 3 mm. cut off tool, cut to the right of
the center line on the tailstock dumbell. Go to
a depth of 1.5 inches. This will form the lip of
the top of the dumbell.

Using a 2 mm. cut off tool, cut down to the left
of the lip to cut off the top.

With the tailstock removed, clean up the surface of the bottom portion of the dumbell.
(Continued on page 9)
Neva Hillard
Turning Heirloom Baby Rattles

Page 9
GVWG

Measure the diameter of the lip of the top piece
and transfer this onto the bottom portion.

Hollow out the bottom portion. Be mindful
that you are working with end grain, so go from
the center out.

As you approach the edge go carefully with
small cuts and test fit frequently to ensure a
good fit with the top portion. This, however, is
not critical as both pieces will be glued together.

When you finish hollowing give it a quick sand
to remove any ridges.

Remove the bottom portion and place the top
portion in the chuck and hollow out.

Glue the edges of both portions.

Put the beads/beans in the bottom portion and
fit to the top portion (which is still in the
chuck). Bring up the tailstock to a tight fit and
leave to dry. The amount of time will depend
on what type of glue is used. Do not use cyanoacrylate as the seal may fail. Two part
epoxy or wood glue is OK.

The second dumbell is now at the tailstock end
and so repeat the procedure to cut off the top
portion, hollow out both portions, glue, put in
the beads/beans and fit tightly between centers
to dry.

When dry finish the rattle by shaping the
dumbells and handle. In shaping the handle I
usually put a bead on either side of the
dumbell. The dumbells can be spherical, oval
or flat, they all look good. For the dumbell you
are aiming for a diameter of greater than 1.67
inches to comply with the safety standards for
baby rattles.

Sand

Cut off leaving a small ‘knob’ on either side
which can be cut off with a saw.

Sand off the ‘knob’ being mindful to maintain
the dome shape.

Finish with beeswax, mineral oil or wipe-onpoly or any other ‘food safe’ finish.
I do not sell my baby rattles but when I give them
away I always advise the parents that it is a commemorative gift and ask that they not give it to the
baby. This is to reduce any liability in the event the
baby could be injured by hitting themselves with
the rattle.
(Continued from page 8)

On the second Saturday of each month, the Guild
sponsors a learning session known as Turning 101.
The focus of these sessions is to introduce new
turners to safe practices through simple projects
that can often be finished in a single session. The
Turning 101 Coordinator is Gerry Vickers who
picks the topics, arranges the instructor for each
session, registers the attendees, gathers the money,
arranges for the materials and then attends the
sessions to help out. A growing number of members of our Guild began their turning through
Turning 101.
All sessions run from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM on the
second Saturday of the month except for the December session which is on the first Saturday. All
sessions are held at the classroom facilities at KMS
Tools, 925 Tupperware Avenue, Coquitlam BC and
cost $25.00 per person per session. Please note
that there are only six spaces in each class assigned
on a first-paid basis and the sessions are restricted
to Guild members only. Unfortunately, Gerry cannot take membership payments at the door. You
must have attended at least one Guild meeting prior where you can join up.
Dates have been booked through 2016 and some
topics have been chosen but keep an eye on the
newsletter for details as they come available.

One of the things that distinguishes our
Guild is our dedication to bringing in
world-class demonstrators to give daylong presentations followed by one or
two days of classes. Art Liestman has
been our demonstrator coordinator
since the inception of the Guild and his
relationship with many of these people
helps immeasurably in getting them to
visit us. To date we have hosted over 80
different presenters. When you consider
that most people only get to see these
wonderful turners by attending a symposium it is simply amazing to have the
chance to spend one or two days with
them to learn their stories, experience
their art, and be guided by their teachings – all at a fraction of the cost of traveling to a symposium.
Here is what we can look forward to over
the next 12 months:
Art tells me that he has several others in the
works so stay tuned …….
Bruce Campbell
Upcoming Demonstrators
Betty Scarpino Oct. 24, 25
www.bettyscarpino.com
Betty was one of our headliners in
West Coast Round-up I in 2004
and her artistic eye is as sharp as
the tools with which she turns. All
AAW members know Betty as the
editor of the AAW Journal which
she guided through a successful
transition to a full-colour publication that is the true “voice” of the
AAW. Betty’s work in very sculptural with beautifully organic lines
which she highlights with surface
texturing and colouring.
Micheal Hosaluk Feb. 20, 21
www.michaelhosaluk.com
Mike is from Saskatoon, Saskatchewan and has visited us before as a
demonstrator. I was lucky enough
to take his class then and enjoyed
every second of it. He also was a
presenter at our third West Coast
Round-up Symposium in 2010. He
has a delightful presentation style
and is a superb turning technician.
He is also world-renowned for his
delightful, whimsical, and amusing
pieces.
Steven Kennard Mar. 12, 13
www.stevenkennard.com
Steven Kennard is a woodturner
and sculptor living and working in
Nova Scotia, Canada. We saw his
work back in the days of the West
Coast Woodturning Competition
where his superb East African
Blackwood boxes charmed us all.
Today he continues to create one-of
-a-kind and limited edition turned,
carved and textured sculptural boxes.
Kurt Hertzog Apr. 16, 17
www.kurthertzog.com
Kurt is the newly elected President
of the AAW and has been a professional woodturner for many years.
He enjoys turning a diverse range
of work and is a popular demonstrator and teacher.
